subject: Calculating standard deviation for estimates of finite population change

messages.author: d3e66d7922711174
messages.subject: Calculating standard deviation for estimates of finite population change
parts:
Hi Murray,


I would like to use my estimates of finite population change calculated using a multi-session model (and the contrast function you explained in a previous email) as a response variable in a regression to determine if annual population change is influenced by several environmental variables. As the values of population change are estimates and the level of variation differs between them, I thought it would be appropriate to use a weighted regression. From what I have read, the most common way that weights are calculated is 1/SD^2. Therefore, if possible, could you tell me how to obtain estimates of standard deviation for my estimates of finite population change? Alternatively, if you could inform me how to calculate sample size, I could use SE*square root(n) (unless it's inappropriate to do that in this case).  


Cheers


Jai


~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Jai Thomas
PhD Candidate, Terrestrial Ecology Research Group
School of Veterinary and Life Sciences
Murdoch University, Western Australia

parts:
I wouldn't go down that route and prefer not to advise you on it, but (i) weighted regression has a bad reputation among my statistical friends (no, I can't give a citation!), and (ii) you probably should use openCR with a model of type JSSAsecrlCL if you want to relate lambda to covariates - it should be easy if your data are already in 'secr' format.
Murray

messages.subject: Re: Calculating standard deviation for estimates of finite population change
parts:
Hi Murray,


Thanks for your advice, I had a feeling you were going to say something like that. At the start I had intended to estimate finite population change using the Pradel type model (non-spatial), however not all trap-lines were operational every year and to use the Pradel model I would be restricted to using data collected from trap-lines that were operational every year, which excludes a fair chunk of data. Sample effort was roughly the same between years, but sample area was not the same for each year as some traps were moved to different areas due to access issues (for the record, I had no involvement in the initial design of the monitoring program). This is what sparked my initial interest in the spatial-capture recapture models, as they appeared to be able to handle this issue without having to discard data. 


I will run the JSSAsecrICL model with my data and then compare the estimates of finite population change with the ones that were estimated using the multi-session model with the contrasts function. If the estimates from both models are similar is it reasonable to assume that the difference in esa between years is not too much of an issue?


Thanks again for your advice, it is much appreciated

Jai
